key_success_factors: Balanced nutrient management based on soil test
Integrated Pest Management (especially for Fall Armyworm)
Ensuring proper drainage to prevent waterlogging
Timely sowing for optimal yield potential
Adequate and timely irrigation, especially at critical stages (CRI, tillering, flowering, grain filling)
Effective weed management (Phalaris minor, broadleaf weeds)
Balanced fertilization based on soil test reports
Monitoring for rusts and aphid infestations

zaid.seasonal_weather_pattern: Intense summer heat (May-June) with temperatures often exceeding 40°C. Low humidity. Pre-monsoon showers are possible towards late June. Water availability is a major constraint.
zaid.weather_aware_planting_timing: Plant immediately after Rabi wheat harvest, typically April 15th - April 30th, to utilize residual soil moisture. Ensure irrigation facilities are available as the crop will face high temperatures.
zaid.weather_aware_harvest_timing: Harvest when 70-80% of pods are mature and dry, typically June 10th - June 25th. Aim to complete harvest before the full onset of monsoon rains to prevent pod shattering and grain spoilage.

weather_alerts.description: Extreme high temperatures during flowering and pod development.
weather_alerts.action: Provide light irrigation during cooler parts of the day (early morning/late evening) to reduce heat stress. Consider mulching to conserve soil moisture and regulate soil temperature.

weather_alerts.description: Insufficient water availability due to high evaporation and limited irrigation.
weather_alerts.action: Prioritize irrigation during critical growth stages (flowering and pod filling). Use drip irrigation if available. Select drought-tolerant varieties.

weather_alerts.description: Pre-monsoon dust storms or strong winds.
weather_alerts.action: Monitor forecasts. Ensure plants are not overly stressed. Post-storm, check for lodging or damage and provide support if necessary.

alternative_options.risk_comparison: Lower water requirement, making it more resilient to monsoon variability. Generally lower market price than maize, leading to slightly lower profit but also lower investment and risk in drier conditions.

Requires less irrigation than wheat, making it a good option for water-scarce areas. Market prices can be volatile but often offer good returns. Good for diversification and breaking cereal-cereal rotation.

actions: Complete sowing of Hybrid Maize (e.g., PMH-1, HQPM-1) by July 20th, ensuring good soil moisture after initial monsoon rains. Use recommended seed rate and spacing.
Apply basal dose of fertilizers (N, P, K) as per soil test recommendations for Kharif Maize during sowing. Ensure proper incorporation.
Initiate first weeding or pre-emergence herbicide application for early-sown Kharif crops (Maize, Bajra) to control initial weed flush.
Monitor fields daily for early signs of pests (e.g., Fall Armyworm in maize) and diseases. Prepare for immediate control measures if necessary.
Perform top dressing with the second dose of Nitrogen (urea) for Kharif Maize, typically 25-30 days after sowing, coinciding with the knee-high stage.
Conduct second weeding or interculture operation for Kharif Maize to manage weeds and aerate the soil. Consider post-emergence herbicide application if weed pressure is high.
Intensify scouting for Fall Armyworm (FAW) in Maize and other common Kharif pests. Implement Integrated Pest Management (IPM) strategies, including biological controls or targeted chemical sprays.
Ensure proper drainage in fields to prevent waterlogging during heavy monsoon spells, which can severely damage crops and promote root diseases.
Provide supplementary irrigation to Kharif Maize if there are long dry spells or an early withdrawal of the monsoon, especially during the critical flowering and grain filling stages.
Continue monitoring for late-season pests and diseases. Pay attention to stalk rot and ear rot in maize, and take preventive measures if conditions are favorable.
Begin preparations for Kharif harvest: clean storage facilities, arrange for labor, and ensure harvesting equipment is in good working order.
Collect soil samples from fields after Kharif crop maturity for soil testing to plan nutrient application for the upcoming Rabi season.
Harvest Hybrid Maize from October 5th - October 25th when grains are physiologically mature (black layer formed) and moisture content is optimal (18-20%). Ensure proper drying before storage.
Clear fields of crop residues after harvest. Consider stubble mulching or incorporating residues into the soil to improve soil organic matter and reduce burning.
Initiate primary tillage (ploughing) for Rabi sowing to prepare a fine seedbed. Ensure proper leveling for uniform irrigation.
Procure certified seeds for Rabi Wheat (e.g., HD 3086, WH 1105) and ensure availability of required fertilizers based on soil test results.
Sow Wheat (e.g., HD 3086, WH 1105) from November 1st - November 20th, ensuring optimal soil temperature and moisture for germination. Use seed drill for uniform sowing.
Apply basal dose of N, P, K fertilizers for Wheat during sowing, as per soil test recommendations. Ensure proper placement of fertilizers.
Apply pre-emergence herbicide for Wheat immediately after sowing or within 3 days to control initial weed growth, especially Phalaris minor.
Monitor weather forecasts for early cold waves. Prepare for potential frost protection measures if temperatures are predicted to drop significantly.
Apply the first irrigation to Wheat at the Crown Root Initiation (CRI) stage, typically 20-25 days after sowing. This is a critical irrigation for yield.
Perform post-emergence herbicide application for broadleaf and grassy weeds in Wheat, usually 30-40 days after sowing, when weeds are at 2-4 leaf stage.
Monitor fields for aphid attacks, especially on young wheat plants. Prepare for insecticidal sprays if infestation levels cross economic threshold.
Continue monitoring for frost alerts. If severe frost is predicted, provide light irrigation in the evening or create smoke cover using farm waste.
Apply the second irrigation to Wheat at the tillering stage, typically 40-45 days after sowing, to support vigorous vegetative growth.
Perform top dressing with the second dose of Nitrogen (urea) for Wheat after the second irrigation, ensuring it is incorporated into the soil.
Scout for rust diseases (yellow, brown rust) in Wheat, especially if weather conditions are humid and cool. Apply fungicides preventively or curatively if symptoms appear.
Ensure proper nutrient availability. If any deficiency symptoms are observed, apply foliar sprays of micronutrients as recommended.
Apply the third irrigation to Wheat at the flowering/grain filling stage, typically 70-80 days after sowing. This irrigation is crucial for grain development and yield.
Continue monitoring for late-season pests and diseases. Pay attention to ear head aphids and powdery mildew. Take control measures if necessary.
Start gathering market intelligence for Wheat prices. Explore potential buyers and market channels to ensure a good price for the harvest.
Prepare harvesting equipment for the upcoming Rabi harvest. Ensure combines or reapers are serviced and ready.
Harvest Wheat from March 25th - April 15th when grains are fully mature and dry (moisture content below 12-14%). Avoid harvesting during unseasonal rains.
Clear fields of wheat stubble and residues immediately after harvest. Consider incorporating residues or baling for fodder.
Initiate primary tillage for Zaid Moong sowing. Prepare a fine and well-leveled seedbed to facilitate uniform germination and irrigation.
Procure certified seeds for Zaid Moong (e.g., MH 421, SML 668) and ensure availability of required fertilizers and irrigation facilities.
Direct-sow fast paying leafy greens like spinach/palak and amaranth to utilize the mild weather before peak heat.
Start nurseries or transplant seedlings of summer vegetables (brinjal, bell pepper, chilli) under mulched beds with drip irrigation.
Prepare raised beds for cucumbers and other vines, incorporating 2-3 tons FYM per acre and installing shade net/trellis support.
Plan staggered sowing of cucurbit crops (cucumber, watermelon, bottle gourd) so harvests spread across late May-June.
Intensify pest scouting for aphids/mites as temperatures rise; deploy sticky traps and neem-based sprays proactively.
Sow Moong (Green Gram) from April 15th - April 30th, immediately after Wheat harvest, to utilize residual moisture and complete the crop cycle before monsoon.
Apply basal dose of fertilizers (P, K, and a small amount of N) for Moong during sowing. Ensure proper seed treatment for disease protection.
Provide light irrigation to Zaid Moong immediately after sowing and during critical growth stages, especially if there is no residual moisture.
Initiate first weeding or apply pre-emergence herbicide for Moong to control early weed competition.
Transplant chilli and bell pepper saplings in the first fortnight while soil moisture is still available; maintain mulching.
Sow watermelons/musk melons on sandy loam patches immediately after a light irrigation; maintain ridge-and-furrow spacing.
Schedule weekly fertigation (N:K rich) for summer vegetables to sustain flowering before monsoon onset.
Provide critical irrigation to Moong during flowering and pod formation stages, as these are highly sensitive to water stress under high summer temperatures.
Monitor fields for yellow mosaic virus (YMV) and pod borers in Moong. Implement control measures, including vector control for YMV and targeted insecticides for pod borers.
Perform second weeding or interculture operation for Moong if necessary, to keep the field weed-free and improve aeration.
Begin preparations for Zaid Moong harvest. Clean storage areas and arrange for labor, as the crop matures quickly.
Harvest early Zaid cucurbits and leafy vegetables in dawn hours to avoid heat stress and preserve quality.
Install shade nets / low-cost tunnels for nursery beds to keep seedlings healthy until kharif planting.
Deep plough fallow fields and incorporate crop residues + FYM so soils rest before the first monsoon rains.
Harvest Moong from June 10th - June 25th, when 70-80% of pods are mature and dry. Harvest before the full onset of monsoon rains to prevent pod shattering and grain damage.
Clear fields of Moong residues. Incorporate residues into the soil to enhance soil fertility and prepare for the next Kharif season.
Conduct final checks and repairs on farm machinery, irrigation systems, and storage facilities in anticipation of the upcoming Kharif season.
Procure certified seeds for the next Kharif season (Maize, Bajra) and ensure availability of required fertilizers and pesticides.
